content: Endometriosis is a chronic and recurring condition that typically arises during a woman’s reproductive years. It is characterized by the presence of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterine cavity. This condition is the leading cause of pelvic pain in women. The growth of this ectopic endometrial tissue is primarily driven by estrogen, which is predominantly produced by the ovaries. As a result, traditional treatment strategies have focused on suppressing ovarian function to manage the disease. However, emerging evidence suggests that immune system dysfunction plays a significant role in the development and progression of endometriosis. This has led to the exploration of alternative treatment approaches, such as targeting inflammation. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of anti-tumor necrosis factor-alpha (anti-TNF-α) therapy in managing endometriosis-associated pelvic pain in premenopausal women. To achieve this, a comprehensive search for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Specialised Register, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO. The initial search covered studies up to August 2009, and an updated search extended to September 3, 2012. Additionally, reference lists of included trials were reviewed, and experts in the field were contacted to identify any relevant studies. The inclusion criteria for this review were RCTs that compared anti-TNF-α drugs with placebo, no treatment, medical therapy, or surgical interventions for pelvic pain associated with endometriosis. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials, selected studies for inclusion, and extracted data using standardized forms. The risk of bias was evaluated based on factors such as sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, and selective outcome reporting. Dichotomous data were reported using risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), while continuous data were expressed as mean differences (MD). Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. Only one trial, involving 21 participants, met the inclusion criteria. This trial evaluated the effects of infliximab, a well-known anti-TNF-α drug, on pelvic pain associated with endometriosis. The results showed no significant reduction in pelvic pain as measured by the Biberoglu-Behrman (BB) score for participants (MD -0.14, 95% CI -0.43 to 0.15) or clinicians (MD -0.14, 95% CI -0.39 to 0.11). Similarly, no significant improvement was observed in pain severity using a visual analogue scale (VAS, 100 mm scale) (MD -5.60, 95% CI -16.10 to 4.90) or in the use of painkillers such as ibuprofen (MD -0.10 g/day, 95% CI -0.30 to 0.10). Furthermore, there was no evidence of an increased risk of adverse events in the infliximab group compared to the placebo group (RR 3.73, 95% CI 0.22 to 63.66). The study also found no clinical benefits of infliximab in reducing endometriotic lesions, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, or pelvic tenderness. Additionally, no trials to date have reported on the cost-effectiveness of anti-TNF-α drugs or the likelihood of disease recurrence. The authors concluded that the findings of this review, which was updated in 2012, remain consistent with the original review published in 2010. There is still insufficient evidence to support the use of anti-TNF-α drugs for the management of pelvic pain in women with endometriosis.
